problemText: When a community chooses where to build a new library, what two types of facts must they check about a candidate site?
choices: The site facts about what color the fence will be and the situation facts about the neighborhood's age.
The site facts about how many people live nearby and the situation facts about the building's color.
The situation facts about the ground itself and the site facts about nearby roads.
The site facts about the ground itself and the situation facts about what surrounds it.
hints: Think about the two questions from Unit 1: what is the ground like here, and what does this spot connect to?
Site and situation are the two categories you learned—one describes the ground, the other describes what is nearby.

problemText: A town is choosing between two lots for a new recreation center. Lot Pine is on high, dry ground with plenty of space, but it is far from most neighborhoods and no bus stops are near it. Lot Oak sits on wet, low ground that floods sometimes, but it is within walking distance of four neighborhoods. Which lot has the better site for a recreation center?
choices: Lot Pine, because high, dry ground is a strong site fact.
Lot Oak, because being close to neighborhoods is a strong site fact.
Lot Pine, because being far from neighborhoods makes a better site.
Lot Oak, because wet ground does not matter as much as good situation.
hints: Use the move-it test: which ground facts would travel with the lot if you picked it up and moved it?
Remember that site means the ground itself—not what is nearby. Does high, dry ground travel with the ground?

problemText: A student says, 'We should build the new swimming pool at the North Field because there is a big, empty space there and the ground is flat.' What is wrong with using only this reason to make the decision?
choices: The reason is wrong because a flat field is never a good site for a swimming pool and should be rejected on safety grounds.
The reason names only site facts and does not check the situation—whether students and families can actually reach the pool.
The reason fails to consider situation because it does not examine whether there are roads, parking, or transportation links to the North Field.
The reason is incomplete because it ignores situation factors such as whether the location is close enough for families and students to access.
hints: A good siting decision requires checking both site and situation. The student only talked about one. Which one did they leave out?
Flatness and empty space describe the ground itself. What else needs to be checked before the choice is complete?

problemText: Southridge is choosing between two lots for a new park. Lot Willow has firm, well-drained ground perfect for walking paths, sits two blocks from a school, and is across the street from a busy neighborhood where many families with children live. Lot Sterling has equally firm, well-drained ground and plenty of space, but it sits next to a highway on-ramp, is thirty minutes' walk from the nearest homes, and has no sidewalk connecting it to the surrounding streets. A parent argues that both lots have equally good sites, so either one would work equally well. Is the parent correct?
choices: Yes. Since both have firm, well-drained ground, the site facts are the same, so the parks would be equally good.
No. Lot Sterling has a better site because it is next to a highway, which makes it easier to reach.
No. Both lots have good sites, but Lot Willow has a much better situation, so it is the better overall choice.
No. Lot Willow has a better site because it is closer to the school.
hints: Identical site facts do not make two lots equally good choices. What else matters just as much?
One lot is close to families and neighborhoods; the other is isolated and far from homes. Does that difference belong to site or situation?

problemText: A community wants to build a new market hall. Three facts are offered as reasons to choose the Canal Street lot: (1) The ground is flat and solid and can support a large building; (2) The Canal Street lot is three blocks from the train station where shoppers arrive; (3) The market hall's roof will be made of recycled metal. Which fact or facts are genuine site or situation reasons that actually support this choice?
choices: All three facts, because they are all true statements that describe the Canal Street lot and its features.
Fact 1 only, because the roof material is about building design and construction, not about the location or ground itself.
Fact 3 only, because using recycled materials is always the most important factor when choosing where to build a market hall.
Facts 1 and 2 only, because they describe the ground and its connection to where shoppers come from.
hints: Remember: a justification must be grounded in a real fact about site or situation, not just any true fact about the place.
Check each fact with the move-it test and by asking: does this describe the ground itself, or what surrounds it? Does it matter for siting?

problemText: Two towns are arguing about which lot would be better for a shared youth center. Riverdale offers Lot M: rocky, uneven ground that would cost $50,000 to prepare for building, but the lot is one mile from Riverdale's town center and has five bus stops within a half-mile radius. Hillside offers Lot H: perfectly flat, easy-to-build-on ground, but it is two miles from Hillside's town center and has only one bus stop nearby—a half-hour walk away. An engineer claims that Lot M's cost to prepare ($50,000) makes it a weaker site than Lot H, so Lot H is the better choice for both towns. Is the engineer correct, and why or why not?
choices: No. The cost to prepare the ground is not a site or situation reason for siting—it is a cost fact. Lot M has a poor site but an excellent situation with five bus stops, while Lot H has a good site but a poor situation with only one distant bus stop.
Yes. The engineer is right because Lot H has ground that does not need expensive preparation, and that will save the towns money on construction, making it the more economical choice overall.
No. The cost fact makes Lot M the better choice automatically because any expense involved in preparing a site makes it unsuitable for a youth center and rules out Lot H as viable.
Yes. Because Lot M is rocky and costs more to prepare, it will never be as good a site as Lot H, even if bus stops nearby make it easier to reach for visitors and participants.
hints: A cost fact is different from a site fact. Cost is about money, not about whether the ground itself is suitable or what the lot connects to.
To choose between Lot M and Lot H, you must evaluate both the site and the situation separately. What makes Lot M's situation strong, and Lot H's situation weak?

problemText: A river's course is the path that a river follows as it flows across the land. Which statement correctly describes whether a river's course is fixed in place forever?
choices: A river's course is permanently locked in one location and does not shift or move at any point in time.
A river's course can shift over a long stretch of time, even though it may look the same for a person's entire life.
A river's course changes suddenly every few years due to seasonal rainfall and weather patterns.
A river's course only changes following a major flood or dramatic event that physically reshapes the land.
hints: Think about the key idea that physical geography is not fixed.
The lesson says the change happens gradually, so it is too slow to notice from moment to moment.

problemText: Two maps of the same valley were drawn 50 years apart. The old map shows a coastline at a particular spot on the edge of the valley, and the new map shows the same coastline now sitting noticeably farther back from the ocean. No sudden storms or dramatic events are mentioned in either map. What does the difference between the two maps most likely show?
choices: The coastline moved suddenly during a single large storm that happened between the two maps.
One of the two maps must contain an error, because a coastline cannot change without a dramatic event.
The coastline wore back gradually over the 50 years, a small amount at a time, adding up to a noticeable difference.
The coastline did not actually change; the two maps just measured the water's edge at different times of year.
hints: The lesson teaches that gradual change happens in small amounts over a long stretch of time, too slow to notice moment to moment.
Look for clues about whether a sudden event is described — the problem states no dramatic events are mentioned.

problemText: A student reads a 40-year-old description of where a river bends as it passes through a wide plain. When the student visits that same river today, she finds the bend sitting in a different location than the old description places it. The student wonders whether the old description was wrong. Based on what you know about gradual change, why might both descriptions actually be correct?
choices: The two descriptions cannot both be correct because rivers remain permanently fixed once they establish their channel, so any difference between the old and new positions proves one account is inaccurate.
The old description was definitely wrong because once a river settles into a channel and follows a path, the water always flows through that same location and cannot shift over time.
Both descriptions are correct only if a major flood event occurred between the two time periods and moved the entire river channel suddenly in one dramatic shift rather than gradually.
The old description was correct for its time, and the new location is correct for today, because the river's course shifted gradually over 40 years.
hints: The lesson explains that a place described long ago can be measurably different from the very same place described today, with no mistake involved.
Think about how small changes, happening many times across a long stretch of time, add up to a noticeable difference.

problemText: A photography club takes a picture of a rocky coastline every spring for 12 years. When they compare the first photo with the last photo, they notice the rocky edge has worn back about 6 feet from the ocean. The photos show no signs of broken rock, collapsed cliffs, or damage from storms in any single year. The club wonders what caused this change. Which explanation best fits the evidence, and why is the alternative explanation weaker?
choices: The coastline wore back gradually through small amounts of erosion each year, and those tiny changes added up over 12 years; a single storm would have left visible damage in one of the photos, which the club did not find.

A single powerful storm must have caused all 6 feet of erosion in one event, because coastal environments change only through sudden, dramatic occurrences rather than slow, steady processes happening across many years.
The water level of the ocean rose significantly during the final year, making the rocky edge appear farther back when it actually remained in the same physical location relative to the land itself.
The club repositioned their camera location or angle between photo sessions, creating the illusion that the coastline moved when the actual landscape stayed exactly where it was in all 12 years.
hints: The lesson contrasts gradual change (small amounts over a long time, no visible damage from a single event) with sudden change (a large difference right after a dramatic event).
Notice what the problem does NOT describe — no mention of storms, broken rock, or any single dramatic moment appears in the 12 years of photos.

problemText: Two aerial maps of a river valley are compared. Map A, made 30 years ago, shows the river running along the base of a hill on the western side of the valley. Map B, made last year, shows the river flowing through the center of the valley, much farther east than Map A shows. A local historian's written record mentions normal rainfall and weather throughout those 30 years, with no unusual floods or storms recorded. Based on the lesson about how physical geography changes, which statement best explains the evidence?
choices: The river's course must have shifted suddenly during a major flood that occurred between the two maps but was overlooked or not recorded by the historian in the written records from that 30-year period.

The river's course most likely shifted gradually over 30 years, moving a little bit at a time; the historian's record of normal weather fits gradual change better than it fits a sudden, dramatic shift.
Map A must be inaccurate because a river cannot move that far eastward unless a large-scale geological event like an earthquake or plate movement reshaped the entire valley structure.

The river itself did not move; instead, the western side of the valley floor gradually sank downward, which would make the river's position appear to shift eastward on the newer map even though the water stayed in place.
hints: Think about what you would expect the evidence to show if the change were gradual versus sudden — does the historian's mention of 'normal' weather throughout the 30 years fit one type of change better?
The lesson teaches that gradual change adds up over a long stretch of time with no single dramatic event needed, while sudden change always involves a single event that is describable.

problemText: A geography class studies three pairs of maps. Pair 1: Two maps of a river made 5 years apart show the river's bend moved only 2 feet, with no dramatic events mentioned between the maps. Pair 2: Two maps made 80 years apart show the same river's bend moved 50 feet, also with no dramatic events mentioned in that time span. Pair 3: Two maps made 3 months apart show a river channel that shifted 30 feet and now has a large new gap with scattered boulders, right after a month of extreme rain and flooding. Which pair of maps shows evidence that matches the definition of gradual change best, and why do the other pairs fit differently?
choices: Pair 1 is too short a time period to show a clear pattern of gradual change; Pair 2 best shows gradual change because it covers a long time with consistent small shifts and no dramatic events, while Pair 3 shows sudden change because the large shift happened in only 3 months right after an extreme flood.

Pair 3 best shows gradual change because the maps were made after a specific weather event that caused measurable erosion; Pair 1 does not show enough change over time, and Pair 2 shows too much change to be gradual.

Pair 2 best shows gradual change because 80 years is a long time and the change is not tiny; a small change (Pair 1) does not prove gradual change yet, and Pair 3 shows sudden change because the large change happened in only 3 months after an extreme flood.
All three pairs show gradual change because none of them mention a sudden earthquake or volcanic eruption, and gradual change is any change that takes longer than one day.
hints: Gradual change is defined as small amounts of change, happening over and over across a long stretch of time — consider which pair best fits 'long stretch of time' and shows no single dramatic event.
Sudden change produces a large difference quickly (in days or months) right after a specific dramatic event; think about which pair matches that pattern instead.

problemText: On a map, a leg is one straight stretch of a route between two points. A route with two turns is made of how many legs?
choices: Three legs, because each turn creates a new segment
Two legs, because the route has two turns
One leg, because a route is a single path from start to finish
Four legs, one for each turn plus two more
hints: Count the straight stretches, not the turns themselves.
Each turn happens at the point where one leg ends and the next begins.

problemText: A map's scale bar is divided into four equal segments. Each segment is labeled to stand for 50 meters in the real world. A hiking path on the map spans exactly three of those segments. How far is the actual hiking path in meters?
choices: 50 meters
150 meters
100 meters
200 meters
hints: Multiply the number of segments the path spans by the distance each segment represents.
Do not add the number of segments to the distance per segment.

problemText: The Riverside Park Map shows a playground marked with a star and a pond marked with a circle. A path runs from the playground toward the bottom of the page to the pond. The map's compass rose shows its arrow labeled N pointing toward the top of the page. In which direction does the path from the playground to the pond run?
choices: North
East
South
West
hints: Look at where the compass rose shows north is pointing on this map.
If north is at the top, what direction is toward the bottom?

problemText: The Pinewood Trail Map shows a parking lot marked with a P and a waterfall marked with a W. Its legend shows a solid line for paved trail and a dashed line for dirt trail. A paved trail runs from the parking lot two scale-bar segments toward the right edge of the page to a junction. From the junction, a dirt trail continues one scale-bar segment toward the top of the page, ending at the waterfall. Each scale-bar segment stands for three miles. The map's compass rose shows its arrow labeled N pointing toward the top of the page. What are the two directions traveled, in order, and the total distance from the parking lot to the waterfall?
choices: Right, then up; total distance is five miles
East, then north; total distance is five miles
North, then east; total distance is nine miles
East, then north; total distance is nine miles
hints: Use the compass rose to find direction for each leg separately, not the page directions alone.
Multiply the number of segments in each leg by three miles, then add the two legs together.

problemText: The Twin Lakes Community Map shows a community center marked with a square and two possible locations for a new park, marked as Site A and Site B. A path to Site A runs two scale-bar segments toward the top of the page from the center. A path to Site B runs three scale-bar segments toward the bottom of the page from the center, then two more segments toward the left edge. Each segment stands for 200 yards. The legend confirms both are paved paths. Which site is closer to the community center, and by how many yards?
choices: Site A is closer by 400 yards
Site A is closer by 200 yards
Site B is closer by 200 yards
Site B is closer by 400 yards
hints: Calculate the total distance to each site separately before comparing.
Site B's distance requires adding two legs together first.

problemText: The Hillside Recreation Area Map shows a ranger station marked with an R, and two destinations: Overlook 1 marked with a triangle and Overlook 2 marked with a diamond. Its legend shows a solid line for main trail and a dashed line for side trail. From the ranger station, a main trail runs three scale-bar segments toward the bottom of the page to Overlook 1. From the ranger station, a side trail runs two scale-bar segments toward the top of the page to a rest shelter, then two scale-bar segments toward the right edge of the page to Overlook 2. Each segment is labeled to stand for 500 feet. A visitor uses the scale bar to check both routes but makes an error: she reads the compass rose as showing north toward the right edge of the page instead of toward the top of the page. How would this error change her conclusion about which overlook is closer, if at all?
choices: The error would make her think Overlook 1 is closer, even though Overlook 2 is actually closer by rotating her mental map and counting the segments in the new orientation
The error would not change her conclusion because segment distances do not depend on compass-rose orientation
The error would make her think Overlook 2 is closer by reversing the position of north, which would swap which route appears shorter when she counts segments again
The error would make both overlooks appear to be the same distance away because reorienting the compass rose would cause the two routes to seem equivalent in total length
hints: Decide whether changing the compass-rose reading affects how many segments each path spans.
Distances are determined by counting segments and multiplying by each segment's labeled value.

problemText: A community planner is gathering information about a piece of land before deciding what to build on it. Which of the following is one of the three kinds of facts a planner must learn about the land?
choices: What the residents think about the land and which land use they prefer
How much money the project will cost and when it can be finished
The shape of the land, the water nearby, and what resources the land offers
The names of the roads that border the land and how old they are
hints: The lesson names three facts a planner gathers before making any decision.
These three facts describe the physical or natural qualities of the land itself, not people's opinions or costs.

problemText: A planner is looking at a flat piece of land with very fertile soil next to a stream that flows all year long. No one has built on this land yet. What land use would match this land's qualities best?
choices: A park, because flat land provides good space and is often used for recreation in communities
A road, because roads need solid ground and must connect different areas to allow travel
Housing, because flat land allows builders to construct stable foundations for buildings
A farm, because the land is flat, has fertile soil, and has a reliable water source
hints: Think about what each land use actually needs. A farm's three main needs are listed in the lesson.
The land has all three things a farm requires. Check whether the other uses fit as well.

problemText: A community has a steep, rocky hillside with almost no soil but a beautiful view over a river. The hillside is too uneven to build a house foundation on, and the ground cannot grow crops. What would be the most sensible land use for this hillside?
choices: A park, since the land does not suit farming or building but can still be used and enjoyed
Housing, since steep rocky ground can be leveled and residents value the scenic view
A farm, since the river provides water and farms can be built on uneven ground
A road, since roads need flat surfaces and can transport goods from the hillside
hints: A park does not need flat, fertile, or dry ground the way other uses do. What does a park actually need?
The steep, rocky ground rules out farming and housing. Does that land have to sit unused?

problemText: A town planner is reviewing two parcels of land. Parcel X is flat with good soil, but it sits right on the edge of a river that floods every spring. Parcel Y is flat with thin, sandy soil that rarely grows crops, but it sits on high ground that has never flooded and already has a road running beside it. The town needs one new farm and one new home. Which parcel should become the home, and which should become the farm? Explain your reasoning using land, water, or resource facts.
choices: Parcel X should be the home because living next to water provides natural resources, and Parcel Y should be the farm because it has a road connection for selling crops and transporting goods
Parcel Y should be the home because it sits on high ground that does not flood and already has a road, but Parcel X cannot be the farm because its flooding makes it unsuitable for crops.
Parcel X should be the farm because the river water is always available for irrigation, and Parcel Y should be the home because roads make it easier for people to access services and travel
Parcel Y should be the farm because sandy soil drains well and prevents water from sitting, and Parcel X should be the home because it has good soil for a stable foundation and strong base
hints: Housing must stay dry and not sit on a floodplain. Which parcel meets this need?
A farm needs fertile soil. The sandy soil on Parcel Y is the opposite of fertile, so what does that mean for making it a farm?

problemText: A resident suggests that the town should place a new park on a flat, dry piece of land with very fertile soil, because the park would have plenty of space and people would enjoy it. A planner disagrees and wants to save that same land for a farm instead. Using the land, water, and resource facts from the lesson, explain which person is thinking about the land use correctly and why.
choices: The resident is correct because parks improve quality of life and communities value recreation and open space for enjoyment
Both are equally correct because parks and farms serve different purposes and both provide value to a community in their own ways
The planner is correct because fertile soil is a resource the land offers, and a farm needs that resource, while a park does not need fertile soil to work well.
The planner is correct because fertile soil can only be used for farming and will be wasted if used for any other purpose
hints: A good planning reason must name a land, water, or resource fact, not just what people would enjoy.
What does a park actually need from the land, and what does a farm need? Is fertile soil one of those needs?

problemText: A planner is deciding how to use four parcels of land. Parcel 1 is flat and sits on a floodplain. Parcel 2 is flat, has fertile soil, and sits next to a stream that flows year-round, but it is located far from any existing road. Parcel 3 is steep and rocky with no soil, but it overlooks a scenic pond. Parcel 4 is flat, stays dry, and is already connected to the main road through town. The town needs a new farm, a new park, and housing for one new family. Parcel 1 will not be used. Which of the remaining three parcels should become the farm, and which should become the housing? What should happen to the remaining parcel?
choices: Parcel 3 should be the farm because it has a scenic view for farmers to enjoy, Parcel 4 should be the housing because it is flat, and Parcel 2 should become the park for recreation
Parcel 2 should be the farm because it is in a remote location away from town, Parcel 3 should be the housing because it overlooks water, and Parcel 4 should become the park for community use
Parcel 4 should be the farm because it is already connected to roads for transporting crops, Parcel 2 should be the housing because it has a stream for water, and Parcel 3 should become the park
Parcel 2 should be the farm because it has fertile soil and water, Parcel 4 should be the housing because it is flat and dry, and Parcel 3 should become the park because it is steep and rocky.
hints: Check what each land use needs, then match each parcel's facts to those needs. A farm needs fertile soil and water; housing needs flat, dry ground; a park can use land that does not suit the other two.
Parcel 2 has fertile soil and a stream, which is what a farm needs. Parcel 4 is flat and dry, which is what housing needs. That leaves Parcel 3 for the park.
